stem: The average weather conditions of a place or region, taken over a long period of time (usually about 30 years or more), is called its:
solution: Climate is the average weather conditions of a place or region, computed over a long period of time (conventionally about 30 years or more). It represents the general, long-term pattern of temperature, rainfall, humidity, winds, etc., that characterises a place — as opposed to the short-term, day-to-day state of the atmosphere. Understanding the definition of climate (long-term average weather) is a fundamental prelims point. Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period (about 30 years or more).

stem: The day-to-day, short-term condition of the atmosphere at a place (in terms of temperature, rainfall, wind, etc.) is called:
solution: Weather is the short-term, day-to-day (even hour-to-hour) condition or state of the atmosphere at a place — described by its temperature, rainfall, humidity, cloudiness, wind, and so on, at a particular time. Weather changes frequently and can differ from day to day. (Climate, by contrast, is the long-term average of the weather over many years.) So weather is the momentary/short-term atmospheric condition, and climate is its long-term average. Understanding the difference between weather (short-term) and climate (long-term) is a fundamental prelims point. Weather is the short-term, day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a place.

stem: The main difference between weather and climate is one of:
options: Time-scale — weather is short-term (day-to-day), while climate is the long-term average (over ~30 years)
solution: The main difference between weather and climate is one of time-scale. Weather refers to the short-term, day-to-day (or hour-to-hour) condition of the atmosphere at a place (which can change rapidly), while climate refers to the long-term average of the weather conditions of a place or region, taken over a long period of time (usually about 30 years or more). In short: 'weather' is what the atmosphere is doing now/today, and 'climate' is the average of what it does over many years. Understanding this time-scale distinction is a key prelims point. Weather is short-term (day-to-day); climate is the long-term average of weather (over ~30 years).

stem: A widely used classification of world climates, based on temperature and rainfall and their effect on vegetation, was given by:
solution: The most widely used classification of world climates was given by Wladimir Köppen (a German climatologist). The Köppen classification is based on the values of temperature and precipitation (rainfall) and their seasonal distribution, and it uses vegetation as an indicator of climate (the climate types broadly correspond to major vegetation types). Köppen used a system of capital and small letters to designate climatic groups and types (for example, 'A' for tropical, 'B' for dry, 'C' for warm temperate, 'D' for cold, 'E' for polar). The Köppen scheme is empirical (based on observed data). Understanding that Köppen gave the widely-used climate classification is a prelims point. Wladimir Köppen gave the widely-used classification of world climates based on temperature and rainfall.

stem: In the Köppen climate classification, the letter 'A' stands for the __________ climates (hot and wet, near the equator).
solution: In the Köppen classification, the capital letter 'A' stands for the Tropical (humid) climates — the hot, wet climates found in the low latitudes near the equator, where the average temperature of every month is above 18°C and rainfall is generally high. These include the tropical rainforest ('Af') and tropical monsoon and savanna types. (Köppen's five major groups are: A — Tropical; B — Dry; C — Warm temperate/mild; D — Cold snow-forest; E — Polar/Ice.) Understanding that 'A' = Tropical climates in Köppen's scheme is a prelims point. In Köppen's classification, 'A' denotes the tropical (hot, wet) climates.

stem: In the Köppen classification, the letter 'B' stands for the __________ climates.
solution: In the Köppen classification, the capital letter 'B' stands for the Dry climates — the arid (desert, 'BW') and semi-arid (steppe, 'BS') climates, where evaporation generally exceeds precipitation (moisture deficiency). These dry climates are found especially in the subtropical high-pressure belts and in continental interiors. (Köppen's five groups: A — Tropical; B — Dry; C — Warm temperate; D — Cold snow-forest; E — Polar. Note that 'B' is defined by dryness/moisture, whereas the others are defined mainly by temperature.) Understanding that 'B' = Dry climates in Köppen's scheme is a prelims point. In Köppen's classification, 'B' denotes the dry (arid and semi-arid) climates.

stem: In the Köppen classification, the letter 'E' stands for the __________ climates.
solution: In the Köppen classification, the capital letter 'E' stands for the Polar (ice) climates — the very cold climates of the high latitudes and polar regions, where the temperature of the warmest month is below 10°C. These include the tundra ('ET') and the ice-cap/perpetual frost ('EF') types. (Köppen's five major groups are: A — Tropical; B — Dry; C — Warm temperate; D — Cold snow-forest; E — Polar/Ice.) Understanding that 'E' = Polar climates in Köppen's scheme is a prelims point. In Köppen's classification, 'E' denotes the polar (ice) climates.

stem: The hot, wet climate found near the equator, with high temperatures and heavy rainfall throughout the year (supporting dense evergreen rainforests), is the:
solution: The equatorial (tropical rainforest) climate is the hot, wet climate found in the low latitudes near the equator (roughly within 5°–10° of it, as in the Amazon and Congo basins and Southeast Asia). It is characterised by consistently high temperatures throughout the year (little seasonal variation, hot all year), and heavy rainfall in every month (abundant convectional rainfall, often as daily afternoon thunderstorms) with high humidity. These hot, wet conditions support the dense, luxuriant, evergreen tropical rainforests. Understanding the equatorial climate (hot and wet all year, rainforests) is a prelims point. The equatorial climate is hot and wet throughout the year, supporting dense evergreen rainforests.

stem: The climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters (rain in winter), found on the western sides of continents around 30°–40° latitude (as around the Mediterranean Sea), is the:
solution: The Mediterranean climate is characterised by hot, dry summers and mild (warm), wet winters — that is, the rainfall comes mainly in winter (unusual, since most places get their rain in summer). It is found on the western sides of continents in the subtropics, roughly between 30° and 40° latitude — around the Mediterranean Sea (hence the name), and also in California, central Chile, the south-western tip of Africa (around Cape Town), and parts of southern Australia. The characteristic vegetation is drought-resistant scrub and evergreen trees. Understanding the Mediterranean climate (dry summers, wet winters; ~30–40° west coasts) is a prelims point. The Mediterranean climate has hot dry summers and mild wet winters, on western coasts around 30–40° latitude.

stem: The very cold, treeless climate of the high latitudes (near the Arctic), where only mosses, lichens, and low shrubs grow during a short cool summer, is the:
solution: The tundra climate is the very cold, treeless climate of the high latitudes — the polar and sub-polar regions bordering the Arctic Ocean (northern Canada, Alaska, northern Siberia/Russia, coastal Greenland). It has extremely long, bitterly cold winters and only a short, cool summer (the warmest month below 10°C); the subsoil is often permanently frozen (permafrost). It is too cold for trees, so only hardy, low-growing plants — mosses, lichens, sedges, and dwarf shrubs — survive (the 'tundra' vegetation). Understanding the tundra climate (very cold, treeless, mosses/lichens) is a prelims point. The tundra climate is the very cold, treeless climate of the high latitudes, with only mosses, lichens, and low shrubs.

stem: Climate change refers to a significant, long-term change in the __________ of a place or of the Earth as a whole.
solution: Climate change refers to a significant and lasting (long-term) change in the climate — that is, in the long-term average patterns of temperature, rainfall, winds, and other elements — of a place, a region, or the Earth as a whole. Climate change is not the same as normal day-to-day weather variation; it means a shift in the underlying long-term climate itself (for example, a general warming of the Earth, or a shift in rainfall patterns) over decades, centuries, or longer. The Earth's climate has changed naturally throughout its history (ice ages and warm periods), but the present concern is the rapid climate change (especially global warming) caused by human activities. Understanding what climate change means is a prelims point. Climate change is a significant, long-term change in the climate (average weather patterns) of a place or the Earth.

stem: The gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans, largely due to the increase of greenhouse gases from human activities, is called:
solution: Global warming is the gradual, long-term increase in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. It is caused largely by the enhanced greenhouse effect — the increase in the concentration of greenhouse gases (especially carbon dioxide, and also methane, etc.) in the atmosphere due to human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas), deforestation, and industry. These extra greenhouse gases trap more of the outgoing heat (long-wave radiation), warming the planet. Global warming is the main aspect of present-day climate change, with serious consequences (melting ice, rising sea levels, extreme weather, etc.). Understanding global warming (rising Earth temperature from greenhouse gases) is a key prelims point. Global warming is the rise in the Earth's average temperature due to increasing greenhouse gases from human activities.

stem: Which of the following is the MOST important greenhouse gas responsible for the recent global warming, released mainly by the burning of fossil fuels?
solution: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the most important greenhouse gas responsible for recent global warming. Although it makes up only a small fraction of the atmosphere, its concentration has been rising rapidly due to human activities — chiefly the burning of fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, and natural gas) for energy, transport, and industry, and also deforestation (which removes the trees that absorb CO2). The extra CO2 traps more outgoing heat, enhancing the greenhouse effect and warming the Earth. (Other greenhouse gases contributing to warming include methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs, and water vapour.) Understanding that CO2 (from fossil fuels) is the chief greenhouse gas in global warming is a key prelims point. Carbon dioxide, from burning fossil fuels, is the most important greenhouse gas causing global warming.

stem: Which of the following is a greenhouse gas (besides carbon dioxide) that contributes to global warming?
solution: Methane (CH4) is an important greenhouse gas (besides carbon dioxide) that contributes to global warming. Although present in small amounts, methane is a very potent greenhouse gas (much more effective, molecule for molecule, at trapping heat than CO2). It is released from sources such as paddy (rice) fields, cattle and livestock (from their digestion), wetlands, landfills/garbage dumps, and the extraction of coal, oil, and natural gas. Other greenhouse gases include nitrous oxide, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), and water vapour. (Nitrogen, argon, and neon are NOT greenhouse gases.) Understanding that methane is a key greenhouse gas is a prelims point. Methane (CH4) is a potent greenhouse gas that, besides CO2, contributes to global warming.

stem: Which of the following is a likely consequence of global warming?
options: Melting of glaciers and ice caps, and a rise in sea levels
A permanent decrease in global temperatures
solution: A likely (and observed) consequence of global warming is the melting of glaciers and the polar ice caps, and a resulting rise in sea levels — which threatens to flood low-lying coastal areas and islands. Other consequences of global warming/climate change include: more frequent and intense extreme weather events (heat waves, droughts, floods, stronger storms); shifts in rainfall patterns and agricultural zones; loss of biodiversity and disruption of ecosystems; and the spread of some diseases. So the correct consequence here is melting ice and rising sea levels (not cooling or expanding ice). Understanding the consequences of global warming is a prelims point. Global warming causes the melting of glaciers and ice caps and a rise in sea levels.

stem: The natural process by which certain atmospheric gases trap heat and keep the Earth warm enough for life is called the:
solution: The greenhouse effect is the natural process by which certain gases in the atmosphere (greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane, etc.) trap heat: they allow the incoming short-wave solar radiation to pass through and warm the Earth's surface, but they absorb much of the outgoing long-wave (heat) radiation emitted by the warmed surface, re-radiating part of it back downward — thereby keeping the lower atmosphere and the Earth's surface warmer than they would otherwise be. This natural greenhouse effect is essential — without it the Earth would be far too cold (frozen) for life. The problem arises when human activities increase the greenhouse gases, enhancing the effect and causing global warming. Understanding the greenhouse effect (natural warming that makes Earth habitable) is a prelims point. The greenhouse effect is the natural trapping of heat by atmospheric gases, keeping the Earth warm enough for life.

stem: The Earth's climate has changed many times in the geological past. The long, cold periods when large parts of the Earth were covered by ice sheets and glaciers are called:
solution: Ice ages (glacial periods) are the long, cold periods in the Earth's geological past during which the average global temperature dropped significantly and large parts of the Earth's surface (especially in the higher latitudes and on mountains) were covered by extensive ice sheets and glaciers. The Earth has experienced several ice ages, separated by warmer 'interglacial' periods; the most recent major ice age ended about 10,000–12,000 years ago. These natural climate changes (ice ages and warm periods) show that the Earth's climate has always changed over long time-scales, due to natural causes. Understanding ice ages (cold, glaciated periods of the past) is a prelims point. Ice ages are the long, cold periods when large parts of the Earth were covered by ice.

stem: The causes of natural climate change (in the geological past) include changes in the Earth's orbit and tilt, variations in the Sun's energy, and:
options: Volcanic eruptions (which put ash and gases into the atmosphere)
solution: The natural causes of climate change (operating over the geological past, independent of humans) include: changes in the Earth's orbit and axial tilt (the Milankovitch cycles, which alter the amount and distribution of insolation over long periods); variations in the Sun's energy output (solar activity, like sunspot cycles); volcanic eruptions (which throw huge quantities of ash and gases — such as sulphur dioxide — into the atmosphere, temporarily blocking sunlight and cooling the Earth); the drifting of the continents (plate tectonics) over very long periods; and changes in ocean currents and in the composition of the atmosphere. (Traffic, radio, and city-building are recent human factors, not natural geological causes.) Understanding the natural causes of climate change (including volcanic eruptions) is a prelims point. Natural climate change is caused by changes in the Earth's orbit/tilt, solar variations, and volcanic eruptions, among others.

stem: The main human (anthropogenic) cause of present-day climate change (global warming) is the increase of greenhouse gases from:
options: The burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas), deforestation, and industrialisation
solution: The main human (anthropogenic) cause of present-day climate change and global warming is the increase of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, resulting from human activities such as: the burning of fossil fuels — coal, oil (petroleum), and natural gas — for energy, transport, and industry (which releases large amounts of carbon dioxide); deforestation (cutting down forests, which removes the trees that absorb CO2 and often involves burning); industrialisation and various industrial processes; and agriculture (e.g., methane from paddy fields and livestock). These human activities have sharply raised the concentration of greenhouse gases, enhancing the greenhouse effect and warming the planet. Understanding the human causes of climate change (fossil fuels, deforestation, industry) is a key prelims point. The main human cause of global warming is greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and industry.

stem: Which of the following measures would help to REDUCE global warming / climate change?
options: Using renewable/clean energy (solar, wind), planting trees (afforestation), and reducing the burning of fossil fuels
solution: Measures that would help to reduce (mitigate) global warming and climate change include: using renewable and clean sources of energy (such as solar, wind, hydro, and other non-fossil-fuel energy) instead of fossil fuels; planting trees / afforestation (trees absorb carbon dioxide, acting as 'carbon sinks'); reducing the burning of fossil fuels and improving energy efficiency; reducing, reusing, and recycling; using public transport; and reducing deforestation. International cooperation and agreements to cut greenhouse gas emissions also help. (Burning more coal/oil, cutting forests, and increasing emissions would worsen, not reduce, global warming.) Understanding the measures to reduce global warming is a prelims-relevant point. Using clean energy, planting trees, and reducing fossil-fuel burning help reduce global warming.

stem: Climatic regions of the world roughly correspond to belts of latitude, because the primary control of climate is:
options: Latitude (which determines temperature through the angle of the sun's rays)
solution: The climatic regions of the world roughly correspond to belts of latitude because the primary control of climate is latitude, which determines the amount of solar energy (insolation) received — through the angle of the Sun's rays and the length of day. As a result, temperature (and broadly, the type of climate) changes systematically from the hot equator toward the cold poles: hot tropical climates near the equator, dry climates around the subtropics, temperate climates in the mid-latitudes, and cold polar climates near the poles. (This latitudinal pattern is then modified by other factors — altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, winds, and mountains.) Understanding that latitude is the primary control of world climate is a prelims point. World climatic regions follow latitude belts because latitude is the primary control of climate.

stem: Besides latitude, other important factors that control the climate of a place include altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, winds, and:
solution: Besides latitude (the primary control), the important factors controlling the climate of a place include: altitude (temperature decreases with height, so highlands are cooler); distance from the sea / continentality (coasts have equable climates, interiors have extreme climates); ocean currents (warm currents warm the coasts they wash, cold currents cool them); prevailing winds (which bring the temperature and moisture of the regions they come from); and relief/topography (mountains — which cause orographic rainfall on windward slopes and rain shadows on leeward slopes, and act as barriers to winds). Together these factors produce the variety of climates over the Earth. Understanding the full set of climate-controlling factors is a prelims point. Climate is controlled by latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, winds, and relief.

stem: The 'monsoon' type of climate (with a marked wet season and dry season, driven by seasonally-reversing winds), which dominates the Indian subcontinent, is a type of __________ climate.
solution: The monsoon type of climate is a type of tropical climate. It is found in the tropical/subtropical regions of South and Southeast Asia (most notably the Indian subcontinent) and is characterised by a marked seasonal reversal of winds (the monsoons): a hot, rainy wet season in summer (when moist winds blow from the sea to the land, bringing heavy rainfall — the south-west monsoon in India) and a dry season in winter (when dry winds blow from the land to the sea). So it has high temperatures (tropical) with a strong seasonal rhythm of rainfall (wet summer, dry winter). Understanding that the monsoon climate is a tropical climate type is a prelims point. The monsoon climate, with its wet and dry seasons, is a type of tropical climate.

stem: Assertion (A): Global warming is causing sea levels to rise. Reason (R): Global warming melts glaciers and ice sheets, and warms (expands) ocean water. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that global warming is causing sea levels to rise. And the reason is (R) that global warming (i) melts glaciers and the polar ice sheets, adding more water to the oceans, and (ii) warms the ocean water, causing it to expand (thermal expansion — warm water takes up more volume). Both of these effects raise the sea level, so R correctly explains A. Rising sea levels threaten to submerge low-lying coasts, islands, and cities. Understanding this cause-effect (warming → melting ice + expanding water → rising seas) is a prelims point. Global warming raises sea levels by melting ice and thermally expanding ocean water.

stem: In the Köppen classification, the letter 'C' stands for the __________ climates (mild winters).
solution: In the Köppen classification, the capital letter 'C' stands for the Warm temperate (mild, or mesothermal) climates — the mild mid-latitude climates in which the coldest month has an average temperature between about 18°C and −3°C (mild, not severe, winters). This group includes the Mediterranean ('Cs'), the humid subtropical/China type ('Cw', 'Cfa'), and the marine west-coast ('Cfb') climates. (Köppen's five major groups: A — Tropical; B — Dry; C — Warm temperate; D — Cold snow-forest; E — Polar.) Understanding that 'C' = warm temperate climates is a prelims point. In Köppen's classification, 'C' denotes the warm temperate (mild) climates.

stem: In the Köppen classification, the letter 'D' stands for the __________ climates.
solution: In the Köppen classification, the capital letter 'D' stands for the Cold snow-forest (microthermal) climates — the cold mid-to-high-latitude continental climates with severe (very cold) winters, in which the coldest month averages below −3°C and the warmest above 10°C. These climates (found in large landmasses of the Northern Hemisphere, like Canada and Russia) support the great coniferous (boreal) forests — the taiga. (Köppen's five groups: A — Tropical; B — Dry; C — Warm temperate; D — Cold snow-forest; E — Polar.) Understanding that 'D' = cold snow-forest climates is a prelims point. In Köppen's classification, 'D' denotes the cold snow-forest climates with severe winters.

stem: The vast belt of coniferous (evergreen needle-leaf) forest found in the cold climates of the high northern latitudes (Canada, Russia/Siberia) is called the taiga or __________ forest.
solution: The taiga (also called the boreal forest) is the vast belt of coniferous, evergreen, needle-leaf forest (pines, firs, spruces) found in the cold 'D'-type climates of the high northern latitudes — stretching across northern Canada, Scandinavia, and Russia/Siberia. These forests are adapted to the long, very cold winters and short, cool summers of the sub-arctic climate. The taiga/boreal forest is one of the world's largest land biomes. Understanding the taiga/boreal forest (coniferous forest of the cold north) is a prelims point. The taiga (boreal forest) is the coniferous forest of the cold high northern latitudes.

stem: The hot, tropical grassland climate with a distinct wet and dry season (found between the equatorial forests and the hot deserts, as in much of Africa) is the __________ climate.
solution: The savanna climate is the hot, tropical wet-and-dry climate found between the equatorial rainforest belt and the hot deserts (roughly 5°–20° latitude), most extensively in Africa (e.g., the Sudan/Sahel region and East Africa), but also in parts of South America, India, and Australia. It has high temperatures all year and a marked seasonal rainfall — a distinct wet season (summer, when the ITCZ brings rain) and a dry season (winter). Its characteristic vegetation is tropical grassland with scattered trees — the savanna — which supports large herbivores and famous wildlife. Understanding the savanna climate (tropical wet-and-dry, grassland) is a prelims point. The savanna climate is the hot tropical wet-and-dry climate of the grasslands between the rainforests and the deserts.

stem: The permanently frozen subsoil found in the tundra and other very cold regions is called:
solution: Permafrost is ground (soil, rock, or sediment) that remains permanently frozen — at or below 0°C — for at least two consecutive years, found in the very cold regions such as the tundra (high latitudes) and high mountains. In such areas, only a thin top layer of the ground thaws in the brief summer, while the subsoil below stays frozen all year (the permafrost). Permafrost affects vegetation (trees cannot root deeply, so the tundra is treeless), drainage (water cannot sink in, creating marshy ground in summer), and construction. Importantly, thawing permafrost due to global warming can release trapped greenhouse gases (like methane), worsening warming. Understanding permafrost (permanently frozen subsoil) is a prelims point. Permafrost is the permanently frozen subsoil of the tundra and other very cold regions.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a greenhouse gas?
solution: Nitrogen (N2) is NOT a greenhouse gas — even though it is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere (~78%), it does not absorb the outgoing long-wave (infrared) radiation and so does not contribute to the greenhouse effect. The greenhouse gases — those that trap heat — include carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), water vapour, ozone, and the chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). So of the options, carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases, but nitrogen is not. Understanding which gases are (and are not) greenhouse gases is a prelims point. Nitrogen is not a greenhouse gas, unlike carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide.

stem: The periodic warming of the surface waters of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean (off the coast of South America), which disturbs weather patterns across the world, is called:
solution: El Niño is the periodic (every few years) abnormal warming of the surface waters of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean, off the coast of Peru/Ecuador in South America. During an El Niño, the normal cold, upwelling waters off South America are replaced by warm water, which alters wind and pressure patterns and disturbs weather across much of the world — for example, it is often associated with droughts (and a weak monsoon) in India, Australia, and Indonesia, and floods in parts of South America. El Niño is part of the larger 'El Niño–Southern Oscillation' (ENSO) phenomenon. (Its opposite — an abnormal cooling of the same waters — is called La Niña.) Understanding El Niño (Pacific warming affecting world weather) is a prelims point. El Niño is the periodic warming of the eastern Pacific surface waters, which disrupts weather worldwide.

stem: El Niño is often associated with __________ (weaker rainfall) of the monsoon over India.
solution: El Niño is often associated with the weakening (or even the failure) of the summer monsoon over India — that is, it tends to bring below-normal monsoon rainfall and increases the risk of drought in India. This is because the warming of the eastern Pacific during an El Niño shifts the atmospheric circulation and the zone of rising air away from the Indian region, tending to suppress the monsoon rains over India. (Its opposite phase, La Niña, is generally associated with a good/strong monsoon.) The link between El Niño and a weak Indian monsoon is important for monsoon forecasting. Understanding the El Niño–weak monsoon connection is a prelims point. El Niño is often associated with a weakened (deficient) monsoon and drought over India.

stem: Which of the following provides evidence that the Earth's climate has changed in the past (allowing scientists to reconstruct past climates)?
options: Tree rings, ice cores, fossils, and rock/sediment records
Nothing — past climate cannot be known
solution: Scientists reconstruct past climates (and find evidence that the climate has changed) using natural records such as: tree rings (the width and pattern of a tree's annual growth rings reflect the temperature and rainfall of each year); ice cores (cylinders of ancient ice drilled from glaciers/ice sheets, whose layers and trapped air bubbles preserve information about past temperatures and atmospheric composition, including CO2 levels); fossils (of plants and animals, which indicate the climate they lived in); pollen deposits; and rock and sediment records (including glacial deposits and features that show former ice ages). These 'proxy' records reveal how climate has varied over thousands and millions of years. Understanding the evidence for past climate change (tree rings, ice cores, fossils, rocks) is a prelims point. Tree rings, ice cores, fossils, and rock/sediment records provide evidence of past climate change.

stem: Ozone-layer depletion (the 'ozone hole') and the greenhouse effect (global warming) are:
options: Two DIFFERENT environmental problems — ozone depletion is the thinning of the ozone layer by CFCs (letting in more UV), while global warming is the trapping of heat by greenhouse gases
solution: Ozone-layer depletion and the greenhouse effect (global warming) are two different environmental problems (though both are related to atmospheric changes and both are of global concern). Ozone depletion is the thinning of the ozone layer in the stratosphere — caused chiefly by human-made chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) — which lets more of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation reach the Earth's surface (causing skin cancer, etc.). The greenhouse effect / global warming, by contrast, is the trapping of the Earth's outgoing heat by greenhouse gases (like CO2 and methane), which warms the planet. So they have different causes, different mechanisms, and different effects — they should not be confused. (International action on ozone depletion is the Montreal Protocol; on climate change, the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement.) Understanding that ozone depletion and global warming are distinct problems is a prelims point. Ozone depletion (UV via CFCs) and global warming (heat trapped by greenhouse gases) are two different problems.

stem: The international agreement (treaty), adopted in 1997, that committed developed countries to reduce their emissions of greenhouse gases, was the:
solution: The Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997 (in Kyoto, Japan), was the international agreement under which the developed (industrialised) countries committed to reduce their emissions of greenhouse gases (like carbon dioxide) by specified targets, in order to combat global warming/climate change. It was a landmark treaty in international climate policy (linked to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). (It was later followed by the Paris Agreement of 2015.) (Note: the Montreal Protocol, by contrast, deals with ozone-depleting substances like CFCs — a different problem.) Understanding the Kyoto Protocol (1997 treaty to cut greenhouse gases) is a prelims point. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) committed developed countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

stem: Forests and oceans, which absorb and store large amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, act as important carbon __________.
solution: Forests and oceans act as important carbon sinks — that is, they absorb and store (soak up) large amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, thereby helping to reduce the amount of CO2 in the air and to slow global warming. Forests take up CO2 through photosynthesis (storing carbon in trees and soil), and the oceans absorb CO2 into their waters and through marine plants. (The opposite of a sink is a 'source', which releases CO2 — such as burning fossil fuels.) This is why protecting forests and the oceans (and afforestation) is important for combating climate change — and why deforestation is doubly harmful (it removes a sink and releases stored carbon). Understanding carbon sinks (forests/oceans absorbing CO2) is a prelims point. Forests and oceans are carbon sinks that absorb and store carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

stem: The hot desert climate (as in the Sahara) is characterised by:
options: Extremely low rainfall (aridity), very high daytime temperatures, and a large diurnal (day-night) temperature range
solution: The hot desert climate (as in the Sahara, Arabian, and Thar deserts) is characterised by: extremely low rainfall (great aridity — often less than 25 cm a year, sometimes almost none), because these deserts lie under the dry, descending air of the subtropical high-pressure belts (~30°); very high daytime temperatures in summer (scorching heat, among the highest on Earth); and a large diurnal (day-to-night) temperature range — very hot days but cold nights, because the clear, dry, cloudless skies allow strong heating by day and rapid heat loss by night. The scanty vegetation is drought-adapted (like cacti and thorny scrub). Understanding the hot desert climate (arid, hot days, cold nights, large diurnal range) is a prelims point. The hot desert climate is arid, with very high daytime temperatures, cold nights (large diurnal range), and very little rain.

stem: The temperate grasslands (like the Steppes of Eurasia, the Prairies of North America, and the Pampas of South America) are found in the __________ of continents.
options: Interiors (mid-latitude continental interiors, far from the sea)
solution: The temperate grasslands are found in the interiors of the continents, in the mid-latitudes, far from the moderating and moisture-bringing influence of the sea (a continental climate). Because they are far inland, they receive only moderate rainfall — enough for grasses but generally too little for dense forests — and they experience hot summers and cold winters (a large temperature range). These temperate grasslands go by different regional names: the Steppes (Eurasia/Russia), the Prairies (North America), the Pampas (Argentina/South America), the Veld (South Africa), and the Downs (Australia). They are important regions for wheat cultivation and cattle/livestock ranching. Understanding that temperate grasslands lie in mid-latitude continental interiors is a prelims point. Temperate grasslands (Steppes, Prairies, Pampas) are found in the mid-latitude interiors of continents.

stem: Which of these is an example of a possible EFFECT of climate change on agriculture?
options: Shifts in growing seasons and crop zones, and reduced yields due to droughts, floods, or heat stress
The end of all farming instantly
solution: A possible effect of climate change on agriculture is the disruption of farming through: shifts in the growing seasons and in the geographical zones where particular crops can be grown (as temperature and rainfall patterns change); and reduced crop yields in many regions due to more frequent and severe droughts, floods, heat waves, and heat stress on crops, as well as changes in the timing and reliability of the monsoon. Water scarcity, new pests and diseases, and soil degradation can also harm agriculture. (Some cooler regions might see some benefit, but overall, climate change poses a serious threat to food production and food security, especially in vulnerable regions like parts of India and Africa.) Understanding the effects of climate change on agriculture is a prelims-relevant point. Climate change can shift crop seasons/zones and reduce yields through droughts, floods, and heat stress.

stem: The cold desert (like the Gobi, and Ladakh in India) differs from a hot desert in that it:
options: Is very cold (freezing) in winter, though it is also very dry (arid)
solution: A cold desert (like the Gobi Desert of Central Asia, or Ladakh in the trans-Himalayan region of India) differs from a hot desert in its temperature: it is very cold — with freezing, harsh winters (and often cool summers) — while still being very dry (arid, with very little precipitation). Cold deserts are dry because they lie either deep in continental interiors (far from moisture sources) or in the rain shadow of high mountains (like Ladakh, in the rain shadow of the Himalayas). So both hot and cold deserts share aridity (very little rain), but they differ in temperature — hot deserts are scorching, while cold deserts are freezing (especially in winter). Understanding the cold desert (arid but cold) is a prelims point. A cold desert (like the Gobi or Ladakh) is very dry like a hot desert, but very cold, especially in winter.

stem: Which region of India is especially vulnerable to a rise in sea level caused by global warming?
options: Low-lying coastal areas and islands (like the Sundarbans delta and the Lakshadweep islands)
solution: The regions of India especially vulnerable to a rise in sea level (caused by global warming) are the low-lying coastal areas and islands — such as the Sundarbans (the low, densely-populated Ganga-Brahmaputra delta region of West Bengal), other coastal cities and deltas (Mumbai, Kolkata, coastal plains), and the low coral islands of Lakshadweep (and the Andaman & Nicobar islands). A rising sea threatens to submerge or flood these low-lying areas, cause coastal erosion, salinise (make salty) the soil and freshwater, and displace the people living there. (High areas like the Himalayas or the Deccan Plateau are not directly threatened by sea-level rise, though the Himalayan glaciers are affected by warming in other ways.) Understanding which areas are vulnerable to sea-level rise is a prelims-relevant point. Low-lying coastal areas and islands, like the Sundarbans and Lakshadweep, are most vulnerable to sea-level rise.

stem: The 2015 international climate agreement in which nearly all countries pledged to limit global warming (aiming to keep the temperature rise well below 2°C) is the:
solution: The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015 (at the Paris climate conference, COP21, under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change), is the international agreement in which nearly all the countries of the world pledged to take action to limit global warming — with the central aim of holding the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Under the Paris Agreement, countries set their own national targets (nationally determined contributions) to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. It succeeded and built on the earlier Kyoto Protocol (1997). Understanding the Paris Agreement (2015, limit warming below 2°C) is a prelims point. The Paris Agreement (2015) is the global climate pact aiming to keep the temperature rise well below 2°C.

stem: The warm temperate climate with hot, humid summers and mild winters, with rainfall in all seasons (or a summer maximum), found on the eastern sides of continents (as in south-east China, south-east USA), is sometimes called the __________ type.
solution: The China type (also called the humid subtropical climate) is a warm temperate climate found on the eastern sides of continents in the subtropics (roughly 25°–40° latitude) — for example in south-eastern China (hence the name), the south-eastern USA, south-eastern South America, south-eastern Australia, and parts of India. It has hot, humid summers and mild winters, with rainfall in all seasons (often with a summer maximum, sometimes influenced by monsoon-type circulation). It contrasts with the Mediterranean type (which is on the western sides of continents at similar latitudes and has dry summers/wet winters). Understanding the China type / humid subtropical climate (east-coast warm temperate) is a prelims point. The China type (humid subtropical) climate is the warm temperate climate of eastern continental margins, with hot humid summers and mild winters.

stem: Building up of pollutants (from vehicles and industries) can cause cities to be warmer than their surrounding rural areas — an effect known as the urban __________ island.
solution: The urban heat island effect is the phenomenon in which urban areas (cities) are noticeably warmer than the surrounding rural (countryside) areas. This happens because cities have lots of concrete, tar/asphalt, and buildings (which absorb and store heat and then release it), less vegetation and open water (so less cooling by evapotranspiration), and they generate additional heat from vehicles, air conditioners, factories, and human activity (plus a blanket of pollutants and dust that traps heat). As a result, the city forms a warm 'island' of higher temperature amid the cooler rural surroundings. This is an example of humans locally modifying the climate. Understanding the urban heat island effect is a prelims-relevant point. The urban heat island effect makes cities warmer than the surrounding rural areas.

stem: The scientific body established by the United Nations to assess the science of climate change and advise governments is the:
solution: The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) is the scientific body established by the United Nations (by the WMO and UNEP, in 1988) to assess the scientific evidence on climate change — its causes, impacts, and possible responses — and to provide governments with scientific information to help them develop climate policies. The IPCC periodically publishes major 'Assessment Reports' that summarise the state of knowledge on climate change and are highly influential in international climate negotiations. (The IPCC does not itself do research, but reviews and synthesises the work of thousands of scientists worldwide.) Understanding the IPCC (UN's climate-science body) is a prelims point. The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) is the UN body that assesses the science of climate change.

stem: The 'marine west-coast' (temperate oceanic) climate, with mild temperatures and rainfall throughout the year (as in north-western Europe/Britain), is found:
options: In the deep interiors of continents
On the western sides of continents in the higher mid-latitudes (~45°–60°), influenced by the westerlies and the sea
solution: The marine west-coast climate (also called the temperate oceanic or 'British' type) is found on the western sides of continents in the higher mid-latitudes, roughly between 45° and 60° latitude — for example in north-western Europe (Britain, France, Germany), the Pacific north-west of North America, southern Chile, and New Zealand. It is dominated by the westerly winds blowing in from the ocean, which give it a maritime (equable) character: mild temperatures throughout the year (cool summers, mild winters — no great extremes) and rainfall spread through all seasons (often cloudy and damp). Understanding the marine west-coast climate (mild, wet all year, western mid-latitude coasts) is a prelims point. The marine west-coast climate is the mild, year-round-rainfall climate of western continental coasts in the higher mid-latitudes.

stem: The retreat (shrinking/melting) of glaciers, including many Himalayan glaciers, in recent decades is regarded as an indicator (sign) of:
solution: The retreat (shrinking and melting back) of glaciers around the world — including many glaciers in the Himalayas (like the Gangotri glacier) — over recent decades is regarded as a clear indicator (visible sign) of global warming and climate change. As global temperatures rise, glaciers melt faster than they are replenished by snowfall, so they shrink and retreat. This glacier retreat is a concern because Himalayan glaciers feed India's major rivers (like the Ganga and Brahmaputra): their shrinking threatens the long-term water supply (and can cause short-term hazards like glacial-lake outburst floods). Glacier retreat is one of the widely-cited pieces of evidence for present-day warming. Understanding glacier retreat as a sign of global warming is a prelims-relevant point. The retreat of glaciers, including Himalayan glaciers, is an indicator of global warming.

stem: In distinguishing weather from climate, which statement is TRUE?
options: A single rainy day changes the climate of a place
Climate is what you expect (long-term average), while weather is what you get (on a particular day)
solution: A true and helpful way to distinguish them is: 'Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.' Climate is the long-term average and expected pattern of atmospheric conditions of a place (over ~30 years) — so it tells you what conditions to expect in a given season. Weather is the actual condition of the atmosphere on a particular day or moment — what you actually get, which can vary from the expected average. So a single rainy or hot day (weather) does not change the climate (which is the long-term average); climate changes only when the long-term pattern shifts. Understanding this distinction is a prelims point. Climate is the long-term expected average; weather is the actual day-to-day condition.

stem: The international agreement (the Montreal Protocol, 1987) was signed specifically to protect the environment by phasing out substances that cause:
options: Depletion of the ozone layer (like CFCs)
solution: The Montreal Protocol (adopted in 1987) is the international agreement signed specifically to protect the ozone layer, by phasing out (banning and reducing) the production and use of ozone-depleting substances — chiefly the chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and related chemicals that destroy stratospheric ozone. It is widely regarded as one of the most successful environmental treaties, as it has led to a marked reduction in these harmful chemicals and the gradual recovery of the ozone layer. (Note the distinction: the Montreal Protocol deals with ozone depletion, while the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement deal with greenhouse gases / global warming — two different problems.) Understanding the Montreal Protocol (ozone-layer protection) is a prelims point. The Montreal Protocol (1987) was signed to phase out ozone-depleting substances like CFCs and protect the ozone layer.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'World Climate and Climate Change' is that:
options: Climate is the same everywhere and never changes

The Earth has a variety of climates (which can be classified, e.g. by Köppen, and which reflect factors like latitude), and the climate changes over time — both naturally (ice ages) and, at present, rapidly due to human-caused global warming, which is a serious global concern
Human beings have no effect on climate
solution: The chapter conveys that the Earth has a great variety of climates — from the hot, wet equatorial climate to the dry desert climates, the temperate and Mediterranean climates, and the cold polar and tundra climates — which can be classified systematically (most famously by Wladimir Köppen, using temperature, rainfall, and vegetation, with groups A, B, C, D, E), and which reflect the controlling factors of climate (chiefly latitude, and also altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, winds, and relief). It further conveys that climate is not permanent but changes over time: in the geological past it has changed naturally (through ice ages and warm periods, caused by changes in the Earth's orbit/tilt, solar variation, and volcanic activity); and at present the Earth is undergoing rapid climate change — global warming — caused mainly by human activities (the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrialisation, which increase greenhouse gases and enhance the greenhouse effect). This human-caused global warming, with its consequences (melting ice, rising sea levels, and more extreme weather), is a serious global concern requiring action (clean energy, afforestation, and reducing emissions). Understanding the classification of world climates and the reality and causes of climate change (natural and, especially, human-induced global warming) is the central concern of this chapter. The Earth has varied, classifiable climates, and its climate changes over time — now rapidly, due to human-caused global warming.
